title: Rows and spaces
hookLine: shoulder to shoulder in rows; men's and women's spaces are arranged differently in different communities
last: MIHRAB — EVERYONE FACES THE SAME WAY.

cards: On a crowded bus or train, how much space do you leave between you and a stranger? Most people leave a gap. A bag on the seat.
An elbow tucked in. A careful few inches that say: not together. Then the call to stand is given in the mosque, and something happens that surprises first-time visitors.
People move toward each other. Strangers close the space, until shoulders touch and the sides of their feet meet. A businessman next to a taxi driver next to a student.

teach.b: Before the prayer begins, the imam often turns and says: straighten your rows, and close the gaps. It comes straight from the hadith.
Bukhari and Muslim report the Prophet ﷺ saying that straightening the rows is part of completing the prayer.

teach.h: SHOULDER TO SHOULDER, FOOT TO FOOT.
teach.b: The companion Anas described what it looked like: each of them would put his shoulder against his companion's shoulder and his foot against his foot.

A report in Abu Dawud tells them not to leave gaps for Shaytan to slip into. Another, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, warns that crooked rows lead to divided hearts. The line on the floor is also a line between people.
And there are no reserved seats. Whoever comes first stands at the front; if the powerful arrive late, they stand at the back. Then the other half of the picture: where do women pray?
In the Prophet's own mosque, women came to the prayers, including the dawn prayer in the dark, and prayed in rows behind the men, in the same room.
Bukhari and Muslim report him saying: do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah. Today the arrangement varies a great deal.
Some mosques have women's rows at the back of the same hall; some have a balcony, a side room, or a screen or curtain.
Around the Ka'ba itself, men and women pray in the same open space. Muslims discuss, and sometimes argue about, which arrangement serves people best, and different communities answer differently.
What doesn't change is the row itself: shoulder to shoulder, no gaps, everyone in it equal.

how: In congregational prayer Muslims stand in straight rows, shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, filling the front rows first; women's spaces are arranged differently in different mosques, from rows behind the men to balconies or separate rooms.

o: the tall tower where the call to prayer is given
a reserved place in the front row for elders
a prayer row, shoulder to shoulder, with no gaps

games.q: what's inside the rows — tap the pairs.
p: shoulder to shoulder, foot to foot
left for Shaytan, says Abu Dawud

s: the Prophet ﷺ said not to prevent women from the mosques
do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah (Bukhari, Muslim).
important people have reserved places at the front
there are no reserved seats: whoever comes first stands at the front.
every mosque arranges women's spaces the same way
some use rows at the back, some balconies, side rooms or screens; communities answer differently.

games.q: you've arrived early at the mosque. a well-known, wealthy man arrives just as the prayer starts. where does he stand?
o: at the front, where there's a place kept for him
at the back, wherever there's room
games.why: there are no reserved seats. whoever comes first stands at the front, and the rows close up shoulder to shoulder.

practice: If someone is with you, stand beside them, shoulders just touching, facing the same way; if you're alone, stand near a wall and let your shoulder rest against it.
Notice the urge to pull in, to make yourself smaller, to leave a safe inch. Let your shoulders settle at their natural width instead, and take up exactly the room you take up, no more, no less.

wordCard.voice: Saff, the prayer row: shoulder to shoulder with no gaps, and the women's and men's spaces arranged in different ways by different communities.

orig.note: Arabic: a row, the straight line of worshippers in prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: close the gap. No reserved seats in the row, and no safe inch. Until tomorrow.
